rv.q: On a purely human one, this is the most thrilling and visceral drama.
The Guilty is short, sharp and bracingly, repeatedly shocking.

Yes, The Guilty is fairly straightforward as a text. Concerning a troubled police call centre operator, it’s writer Chloe Moss’s adaptation of the Danish film Den Skyldige and its Jake Gyllenhaal-starring Hollywood remake. You could probably have a fairly good time taking a version to the Edinburgh Fringe.
The Guilty is a masterclass in tension and control.
A step above the film, this is a gripping, high-stakes triumph – more than worth leaving the sofa for.
The creative team combine efforts to completely submerge the audience in the apprehension and rapidly increasing anxiety rippling from the stage.
I couldn’t suspend my disbelief, so I was always distanced from what is undoubtedly an extraordinarily gripping and clever piece.
Now, in a taut stage adaptation at the Donmar, Russell Tovey delivers a solo tour de force as Joe, answering calls on a shift fraught with life-and-death decisions.
This is an anxiety-inducing 70 minutes that rarely lets the audience relax.

cn.t: This claustrophobic 70-minute thriller earns strong praise for its nail-biting tension and Russell Tovey's gripping solo performance, though some find the adaptation from film doesn't fully justify the theatrical treatment.
